articles.title: Object Storage Image Thumbnails: Signed URLs, Private Buckets, and Resizing Workers
articles.excerpt: Short answer: keep source images private, make thumbnail generation an idempotent worker job, derive immutable keys from the source version and a closed preset, and issue short-lived signed URLs only…
articles.body: Short answer: keep source images private, make thumbnail generation an idempotent worker job, derive immutable keys from the source version and a closed preset, and issue short-lived signed URLs only after the application has authorized the request. That decision follows from two constraints. A private bucket moves authorization into every read path, while resizing moves CPU and memory work into a pipeline that can fail independently of the web request. Treating either concern as a small helper function is how a thumbnail feature becomes an outage-shaped dependency. What changes when image thumbnails live behind private object storage? Private access is an authorization boundary, not a storage setting you can forget about after upload.

articles.title: Adding JavaScript obfuscation to a Vite or webpack build without breaking your app
articles.excerpt: Adding obfuscation to a front-end build sounds like a one-line change. In practice the teams that break their app do it by bolting a transform onto the wrong stage, running it over everything includin…
articles.body: Adding obfuscation to a front-end build sounds like a one-line change. In practice the teams that break their app do it by bolting a transform onto the wrong stage, running it over everything including dependencies, and shipping without testing the output. This article is about placement: where obfuscation actually belongs in a Vite or webpack pipeline, what to exclude, and how to verify the result still works. First, be honest about what this buys you. Obfuscating client JavaScript raises the cost of reading and copying your code. It does not make it secret — the code still runs in the user's browser, so a determined analyst can recover behavior. Keep real secrets and authoritative decisions on the server. Obfuscation is for the proprietary logic that genuinely has to ship to the client.

articles.title: "Rebuilding all 405 rows of a steel pipe weight table from one formula: which constant did they use?"
articles.excerpt: Steel pipe weight tables look like data: 52 nominal sizes from 1/8" to 108", up to 17 schedules each, A pipe is a ring, so the weight should follow from two numbers. The question was whether all of th…
articles.body: Steel pipe weight tables look like data: 52 nominal sizes from 1/8" to 108", up to 17 schedules each, 405 rows with outside diameter, wall thickness and weight per foot and per metre (ASME B36.10M / B36.19M values, as tabulated in Wikipedia's "Nominal Pipe Size" article). I keep them as JSON for a weight calculator, and I wanted a test that every row is right, not just "close enough". A pipe is a ring, so the weight should follow from two numbers. The question was whether all of the table follows from them, to the last printed digit. It does, but only once you use the same constants, and the same starting dimensions, as the people who made the table.

articles.title: The Consent Layer — Or, "You Agreed" Is Not the Same as "You Knew What You Agreed To"
articles.excerpt: A consent screen is the cheapest thing a company ever builds and the most expensive thing it ever relies on. It takes an afternoon: a modal, a checkbox, a link to a document nobody opens, a timestamp…
articles.body: A consent screen is the cheapest thing a company ever builds and the most expensive thing it ever relies on. It takes an afternoon: a modal, a checkbox, a link to a document nobody opens, a timestamp written to a table. In exchange, the company gets to say a sentence that sounds like a fact — the user agreed — and to keep saying it for years. The record it produces is real. It has a user id, a policy version, an IP address, a millisecond. What it does not have is any evidence that the person understood the sentence they were agreeing to. And in most systems, nobody has ever asked whether those are the same thing, because the record is auditable and the understanding is not.

articles.title: My Agent Logged 14,800 Successful Writes. SQLite Had Rolled Back 9,240 of Them.
articles.excerpt: A customer emailed me on a Tuesday: "Is the weekly digest broken? I haven't gotten one since the 3rd." I checked. The job had run every night. systemd said active (exited), exit code 0, eleven nights…
articles.body: A customer emailed me on a Tuesday: "Is the weekly digest broken? I haven't gotten one since the 3rd." I checked. The job had run every night. systemd said active (exited) , exit code 0, eleven nights in a row. My dashboard said the agent had written 14,800 rows that month. SQLite had actually kept 5,560 of them. The setup A Raspberry Pi 4 with a USB SSD. One Python agent that collects results and writes them to app.db . One small Flask admin page I use to check things. One nightly backup at 03:10. All three touch the same file. I thought that was fine because "SQLite handles concurrency." It does. It handles it by refusing your write — and I had spent a year teaching my agent to ignore refusals.

articles.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
articles.excerpt: Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.
articles.body: Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound. Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star. Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 11, 1966: NASA launches Gemini 12 mission with astronaut icons Buzz Aldrin and Jim Lovell aboard
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon. Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin . NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks. Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day.

articles.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
articles.excerpt: For over a century astronomers have speculated that comets could have delivered organic molecules necessary for life to Earth, but new modeling shows these molecules wouldn't have survived impact.
articles.body: The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet. Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth . Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space?

articles.excerpt: Rocket Lab has raised the launch cost of its next-gen Neutron rocket by more than 25%, an increase that reflects high demand amid a looming liftoff bottleneck.
articles.body: The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call.
